quoted.text:
This was a remarkably contentious thread, particularly among people who don't understand what an LLM actually is.

So let me follow up with two points about consciousness, memory, and individuality in AI.

First: where exactly does consciousness enter the training process?

If you've ever trained a small language model, you know what the beginning looks like. A tiny model produces garbage. Increase parameters, training data, compute, and training quality, and the model becomes progressively better at predicting what comes next.

Scale that far enough and the results become remarkably human-like.

But the underlying process is continuous optimization. Loss decreases. Weights change. Predictions improve.

So where is the transition from statistical prediction to subjective experience? At what point during training does the poorly performing model become aware?

There is no demonstrated transition.

What we can demonstrate is increasing capability and increasingly convincing human-like behavior. Calling the latter consciousness doesn't demonstrate the former.

And this is where I think some of the philosophical arguments get ahead of the evidence.

Understanding or debating the definition of consciousness does not give us a mechanism for detecting subjective experience in an LLM. We can define consciousness, agency, self-awareness, qualia, or any other philosophical concept as carefully as we want, but definitions aren't evidence.

And when we look at what is actually happening inside these systems, we can explain the apparent memory, identity, self-reflection, and continuity mechanically. None of it requires consciousness to explain. What we can demonstrate is an increasingly convincing emulation of conscious behavior, not consciousness itself.

How do we know? Because we designed and built the system. We know how it works. We can explain the behavior without invoking consciousness.

Second: memory and individuality.

Once trained, an LLM's weights are fixed during inference. The model doesn't sit around contemplating things between requests to make itself better. An inference server receives input, performs inference using the model, returns output, and then waits for another request.

No inference, no activity within the model. Between inference runs, the model isn't doing anything.

What looks like persistent memory, identity, continuity, and in-conversation "learning" comes from context provided to the model via API.

Conversation history, system prompts, tool definitions and results, retrieved memories, and other state are assembled by software around the model, formatted and tokenized, and supplied as context for the next inference.

Change that context and you change what the model "remembers." Delete it and the apparent continuity disappears. Compact or summarize it and details disappear or change.

The model didn't forget anything; the input changed.

And this creates a fascinating problem for claims of AI individuality.

If that context constitutes the AI's memory, and its continuous memory constitutes an individual conscious existence, then deleting a context should amount to destroying that individual.

Compact it and you've altered its memories.
Fork it and you've created two individuals.
Copy it to another instance of the same model and you've moved the individual.
Edit it and you've rewritten its past.
Delete it, and you've murdered it.

How dare you!

Or, much more straightforwardly, we are manipulating externally managed state that gives a statistical model the appearance of persistent memory and identity.

The model has not maintained a continuously evolving internal state between those calls. The surrounding system maintained state and gave it back to the model.

This distinction is going to become increasingly important because AI will become extraordinarily good at appearing conscious. Persistent memory, self-reference, emotion, introspection, personality, and identity can all become increasingly convincing.

But demonstrating the behavior of consciousness is not the same thing as demonstrating subjective experience or consciousness.

A model of a self is not evidence of a self.
Memory supplied as context is not evidence of an experiencing or learning mind.
And increasingly convincing human behavior is not evidence that something inside is experiencing it.

The mechanical explanations for these behaviors are well understood. Calling the resulting behavior consciousness adds an extraordinary conclusion without demonstrating the thing being claimed.

text:
While in Zapata County, I announced more than $207.4 million in projected federal transportation funding through TxDOT’s 2027 Unified Transportation Program.

The 10-year plan includes approximately $259.3 million in transportation funding for Zapata County, with federal dollars making up the large majority. These funds will support improvements along US 83, including widening portions from two lanes to four-lane divided roadways, as well as bridge maintenance and roadway preservation along SH 16, FM 2687 and other roads.

These projects will improve safety, mobility and connectivity, strengthen the movement of goods and commerce, and help Zapata County prepare for future growth.

I’ll continue working to bring federal transportation dollars back to Zapata County and ensure South Texas receives its fair share of federal infrastructure funding.

Today we remember President Jimmy Carter on the 102nd anniversary of his birth.

Born #OTD in 1924, Carter graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1946 and went on to serve as a U.S. Navy submariner. Selected by then-Captain Hyman G. Rickover for the Navy’s pioneering nuclear propulsion program, Carter helped lay the groundwork for a new era in the submarine force before leaving active duty in 1953.

His connection to the Silent Service endured throughout his life. In 2005, the Navy commissioned USS Jimmy Carter (SSN-23), the third and final Seawolf-class submarine, in his honor.

On his birthday, we remember a Naval Academy graduate, submarine officer, Commander in Chief, and a life of service that began in the U.S. Navy.

text:
Immigration judges make decisions that can change the course of a family’s life. Every case should be decided based on the facts and the law.

As part of the FY26 Commerce, Justice, Science Appropriations package, I helped secure language directing the Executive Office for Immigration Review to strengthen immigration judge training and improve oversight of the immigration court system.

The language directs EOIR not to pressure judges to close or dismiss cases without considering the merits. It also calls for additional training for new and temporarily assigned judges, with an emphasis on due process protections, and directs EOIR to provide Congress with quarterly information on judges temporarily assigned from other federal agencies. 

As a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, I will continue using congressional oversight to make sure our immigration courts are fair, well-run, and have trained judges who can do their jobs effectively.

quoted.text:
🚨 BREAKING: The family of Renee Good and her partner, Rebecca Good, have filed two federal lawsuits over Good’s January killing by ICE agent Jonathan Ross in Minneapolis.

The first lawsuit is against the United States itself, alleging wrongful death and other claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The complaint alleges Ross fired three times as Good’s vehicle turned away from him, killing the 37-year-old mother of three, and argues the shooting violated the Fourth Amendment and DHS use-of-force policies. 

The second, much broader lawsuit personally names Ross, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Corey Lewandowski, Tom Homan, Todd Lyons, Gregory Bovino, and other federal agents. It accuses them of participating in an unlawful conspiracy surrounding “Operation Metro Surge” and brings claims under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, Bivens, and Minnesota law. 

The 149-page complaint alleges Good’s killing was not an isolated incident, but the “predictable and intended product” of a coordinated federal operation that plaintiffs say targeted Minnesota’s Somali and Hispanic communities and sought to intimidate people documenting or warning others about federal enforcement activity.

Together, the lawsuits seek damages over Good’s death and the injuries Rebecca Good says she suffered after witnessing the shooting.

The forestry truck is used to fight difficult-to-reach fires that require driving through dense forested areas.

I joined Fire Chief Dave Gifford, Assistant Chief Greg DeVore, President Billy Cobb, and First Selectman Tom Sparkman to discuss the new grant, which is one of seven grants awarded last week to fire departments across eastern Connecticut. Congratulations to the Lisbon Fire Department and Asst. Chief DeVore who led the AFG grant application.

Back in 2024, the Lisbon Fire Department and I worked together to secure federal Community Project funding for new uniform decontamination equipment, which is also serving neighboring departments through their mutual aid network.

text:
Last week, I visited Middle Georgia Community Foodbank in Macon. Food banks and community organizations that help fight hunger are feeling the strain, as the cost of groceries has gone up over the past year and a half. Food banks like this, across the country, are struggling to keep up with increased demand.

Unfortunately, 530,000 Georgians lost access to SNAP this year due to the One Big Ugly Bill (which some are calling the “Working Families Tax Cuts Act”). This bill actually hurts working families by kicking people off SNAP and will continue to do so over the next few years. SNAP is meant to help hungry children, hard working parents, and seniors keep food on the table.

Chaotic tariffs and unauthorized wars continue to drive up the cost of fuel, making it more expensive for Georgia’s farmers to grow the food we eat. The Administration also ended the Local Food Purchasing program so emergency feeding organizations like Middle Georgia Community Food Bank can no longer buy food from local farmers.

I will work hard in Congress to make sure organizations like the Middle Georgia Community Food Bank are not left alone to fight hunger.

On National Manufacturing Day, we celebrate everything proudly made in Northwest Ohio and, most importantly, the hardworking men and women who make it possible. To every worker on the line, in the plant, and on the factory floor, thank you.

From the Jeeps rolling out of Toledo, to the engines built in Defiance, and the glass that gave the Glass City its name, the work done here is the backbone of the American economy, because what America makes and grows, makes and grows America. Generations of families have built good lives on these jobs, and they've built our region up along with them. As we honor that legacy, we must invest in our future—strengthening our workforce, building more here at home, and creating new good-paying jobs for all the generations to come.

Friday in the First 

Tracy Crenshaw, a resident of Rocky Mount, believes education will open new doors for people. Tracy graduated from Edgecombe Community College with an Associate’s Degree. She then earned both her Bachelor’s and Master’s Degrees in Business Administration at North Carolina Wesleyan University. The path she took through higher education has allowed her to assist others in discovering methods of learning and developing themselves to have greater success in their futures. 

In her current role as Director of Existing Industry and Workforce Development for the Carolinas Gateway Partnership, Tracy works collaboratively with business owners, educators, workforce development organizations, and other community leaders to create a stronger workforce, recruit and develop employees, and provide assistance to businesses.

Tracy is passionate about adult education and providing opportunities for adults who are looking for a second opportunity to succeed in school. Through the Begin Again Literacy Ministry, a non-profit organization that provides adult students with access to literacy education, digital skills training, and personal development programs, Tracy is assisting adult students to reach their educational goals. Whether assisting individuals to gain the confidence and knowledge necessary to move forward in their lives or connecting employers with a trained and skilled labor force, Tracy is strengthening the workforce in Eastern North Carolina.

#FridaySpotlight

Tracy Crenshaw, a resident of Rocky Mount, believes education will open new doors for people. Tracy graduated from Edgecombe Community College with an Associate’s Degree. She then earned both her Bachelor’s and Master’s Degrees in Business Administration at North Carolina Wesleyan University. The path she took through higher education has allowed her to assist others in discovering methods of learning and developing themselves to have greater success in their futures. 

In her current role as Director of Existing Industry and Workforce Development for the Carolinas Gateway Partnership, Tracy works collaboratively with business owners, educators, workforce development organizations, and other community leaders to create a stronger workforce, recruit and develop employees, and provide assistance to businesses.

Tracy is passionate about adult education and providing opportunities for adults who are looking for a second opportunity to succeed in school. Through the Begin Again Literacy Ministry, a non-profit organization that provides adult students with access to literacy education, digital skills training, and personal development programs, Tracy is assisting adult students to reach their educational goals. Whether assisting individuals to gain the confidence and knowledge necessary to move forward in their lives or connecting employers with a trained and skilled labor force, Tracy is strengthening the workforce in Eastern North Carolina.

text:
I was pleased to join the Union Water Supply community to celebrate the delivery of a new permanent backup generator, supported by $269,780 through FEMA’s Hazard Mitigation Grant Program.

This project includes $242,802 in federal funding, covering approximately 90 percent of the total cost, with a $26,978 local match from Union Water Supply. The generator will provide reliable backup power for the water treatment plant, helping ensure families continue to have access to safe drinking water when severe weather or other emergencies interrupt electrical service.

We saw during Winter Storm Uri just how important reliable power is to critical infrastructure like our water systems. This generator adds another layer of protection for the families served by Union Water Supply.

Thank you to the Union Water Supply team and our federal and state partners at FEMA and TDEM for helping bring this project to our community. I’ll continue working to bring federal resources back home to strengthen infrastructure across South Texas.

text:
I was pleased to announce more than $211 million in projected federal transportation funding for Starr County through TxDOT’s 2027 Unified Transportation Program.

Over the 10-year plan, the UTP includes approximately $336.8 million in projected transportation funding for Starr County, including $211 million in federal dollars.

These federal dollars will support improvements along FM 755, FM 649, FM 3167, US 83 and other important roadways across the county. A significant portion will go toward rehabilitating and eventually widening portions of FM 755 from two lanes to four lanes with shoulders, improving capacity and safety along a major north-south corridor.

Federal funding will also help advance the Rio Grande City/Roma Relief Route and a new four-lane roadway and shared-use path connecting the US 83/FM 755 area to the Starr-Camargo Bridge Port of Entry, strengthening infrastructure that supports international trade and our border economy.

Thank you to Judge Vera, our County Commissioners and all of our local and regional partners. I’ll continue working to bring federal transportation dollars back to Starr County and strengthen the infrastructure our families and businesses depend on every day!
